name: Namchi
tagline: Sky-high town of the Guru statue, Char Dham and Tendong Hill
meta_description: Namchi, South Sikkim: Samdruptse, Char Dham at Solophok, the Tendong Hill trek, local food, shared jeep fares from Siliguri and budget hotels.
summary: Namchi is the headquarters town of Namchi district, the old South Sikkim, at about 1,675 m. It is known for the 118 ft Guru Padmasambhava statue at Samdruptse, the Char Dham pilgrimage complex at Solophok and the Lepcha sacred peak of Tendong Hill. It is 100 km from Siliguri, with frequent shared jeeps.

local_story.title: Sky high, and the hill that saved the Lepchas
paras: Namchi is usually explained as "sky high" in the Bhutia language: nam for sky, chi for top. The name fits a town spread along a ridge at about 1,675 m, looking west over the Rangeet valley towards the hills of West Sikkim and Darjeeling. For a long time it was a quiet market and administrative town for the south of the old kingdom, and after Sikkim became a state of India in 1975 it served as headquarters of South district, renamed Namchi district in 2021. Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities have farmed these slopes for generations.

Behind the town rises Tendong Hill, at about 2,600 m. Lepcha elders tell that long ago a great flood covered the land and the Lepcha people climbed Tendong to escape it. As the waters rose, the hill rose with them, the local story goes, until prayers and offerings made the flood recede. Tendong is often translated from Lepcha as "upraised horn". Lepcha communities remember this every year on 8 August with Tendong Lho Rum Faat, a day of prayers to the hill, and the festival has become a public holiday in Sikkim.

From the late 1990s Namchi set out to become a pilgrimage town. In 1997 the 14th Dalai Lama laid the foundation of a 118 ft statue of Guru Padmasambhava, the teacher who brought Buddhism to Sikkim, on Samdruptse, the "wish-fulfilling hill". It was completed in 2004. The local story is that Samdruptse is a sleeping volcano, and that monks go up to pray to keep it calm. In 2011 Char Dham opened at Solophok, a Hindu complex built around a 108 ft Shiva, so Namchi now draws Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims alike.

did_you_know: The Dalai Lama laid the foundation of the 118 ft Guru Padmasambhava statue at Samdruptse in 1997; the statue was completed in 2004.
Char Dham at Solophok, opened in 2011, has replicas of Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram and all 12 jyotirlingas around a 108 ft Shiva.
Tendong Lho Rum Faat, the Lepcha festival honouring Tendong Hill for saving their ancestors from a great flood, is observed every 8 August.
intro: Namchi is a working district town rather than a holiday village, and that is part of its value: frequent shared jeeps, plenty of hotels at fair prices, a busy bazaar and a mild climate at about 1,675 m. Its two big sights sit on the hills around it. Samdruptse, with the Guru Padmasambhava statue, is a short drive up one side of town, and Char Dham at Solophok a short drive up the other. On clear days in autumn and winter, Kanchenjunga shows to the north-west.

Most travellers give Namchi one night, pairing the two statues in a morning, and then move on to Ravangla, Temi or Pelling. A second night lets you walk up Tendong Hill from Damthang for one of the widest views in South Sikkim, or spend an evening in the bazaar trying sel roti, momos and churpi. Namchi is also a sensible first stop from Siliguri or Darjeeling: 3.5–4 hours by jeep, and an easy link onward to Jorethang and West Sikkim.

highlights.title: Samdruptse and the Guru statue
highlights.text: A 118 ft statue of Guru Padmasambhava, seated on a lotus, on a hilltop a short drive from town. The foundation was laid by the Dalai Lama in 1997 and the statue finished in 2004. Clear mornings bring views of the Kanchenjunga range and the Rangeet valley.

highlights.title: Char Dham at Solophok
highlights.text: Opened in 2011, Siddheshwar Dham gathers replicas of the four great Hindu dhams and all 12 jyotirlingas around a 108 ft seated Shiva on a hilltop. It is clean, well signposted and easy for older pilgrims, with ramps and steps. Allow 1.5–2 hours.

highlights.title: Tendong Hill
highlights.text: The sacred Lepcha hill behind Namchi rises to about 2,600 m. A forest trail from Damthang climbs to the top in roughly 3 hours, where a watchtower gives views across Sikkim and, on clear days, to the Kanchenjunga range and the plains far to the south.

highlights.title: Rock Garden and Ngadak Monastery
highlights.text: Two easy stops near town. The Rock Garden is a landscaped park of paths, pools and flower beds on a slope, popular with local families on weekends. Ngadak Monastery is an old gompa close to the town centre, quiet on most days and worth a short visit.

highlights.title: The bazaar and its food
highlights.text: Namchi's market is where South Sikkim shops. Look for sel roti and tea in the morning, momos and thukpa at lunch, and stalls selling churpi, dried chillies, pickles and large cardamom. Prices are lower than in Gangtok or Pelling and portions are generous.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Namchi through the day, mostly in the morning, for about ₹250–350 a seat and 3.5–4 hours via Melli or Jorethang. From Jorethang it is 45 minutes and ₹60–90. Shared jeeps also link Namchi with Ravangla (about ₹80–120, 1 hour) and Gangtok (about 3 hours). Book seats a day ahead in holiday weeks.

A small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs roughly ₹4,000–5,000 for the 100 km run. From Darjeeling, a car via Jorethang takes about 3 hours. Within Namchi, a local taxi for Samdruptse and Char Dham together costs about ₹1,500–2,500 for a half day; agree the stops and waiting time before you start.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the nearest airport Bagdogra, both close to Siliguri and about 100 km from Namchi. From either, take a shared jeep from the Siliguri stands or a reserved car. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, issued online or at Melli or Rangpo; check current status.

where_to_stay: Most hotels are in and around the central bazaar and along the main roads near the jeep stand, which keeps you close to food and transport; budget rooms run about ₹1,200–2,500 a night and mid-range hotels more. Hotels on the roads towards Samdruptse and Solophok are quieter and some have mountain views, but you will need taxis. Family homestays in the villages around Namchi give home cooking and fields outside the window. For a cooler, quieter night with similar sights, many travellers sleep in Ravangla, an hour away, and visit Namchi on the way.
tips: See Samdruptse and Char Dham in one morning by taxi, starting early for clearer mountain views and smaller crowds.
Remove shoes and dress modestly at Char Dham, and use the official shoe counters rather than leaving them on the steps.
Start the Tendong Hill walk from Damthang by 7 am, carrying water and food, since there are no shops on the trail.
Try sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread, with tea at a bazaar stall in the morning, when it is fresh from the oil.
Plan around 8 August if you want to see Tendong Lho Rum Faat, and expect rain and busy roads on the day.

experiences.title: Samdruptse and the Guru Rinpoche statue
experiences.summary: Drive up to Samdruptse, the wish-fulfilling hill above Namchi, to stand below the 118 ft statue of Guru Padmasambhava, walk the prayer-flag paths around it and, on a clear morning, look across to the Kanchenjunga range. Best early, before the day trippers and the cloud.
body: Samdruptse is a hilltop a short drive from the Namchi bazaar. Its name is usually translated as the "wish-fulfilling hill". On top stands a statue of Guru Padmasambhava, also called Guru Rinpoche, the eighth-century teacher credited with bringing Buddhism to Tibet and Sikkim and blessing Sikkim as a hidden valley. The statue is about 118 ft tall and seated on a lotus base, facing out over the valley. The 14th Dalai Lama laid its foundation in 1997 and it was completed in 2004.

From the car park, paths and steps lead through gardens and prayer flags to the base of the statue, where pilgrims walk clockwise and turn prayer wheels. On clear mornings from October to April the Kanchenjunga range appears to the north-west and the Rangeet valley falls away below; by late morning the hills often haze over. The local story is that the hill is a sleeping volcano, and that monks climb it to pray and keep it calm.

Entry is a small fee, roughly ₹50–100 for Indians and more for foreign nationals; timings and fees change, so check current status before you travel. Most visitors come by taxi, often combining Samdruptse and Char Dham in a half day for about ₹1,500–2,500. Wear shoes with grip, since paths and steps can be wet with dew in the early morning, and carry a light jacket for the wind on top.

faqs.q: How tall is the Samdruptse statue in Namchi?
faqs.a: The Guru Padmasambhava statue at Samdruptse is about 118 ft, or 36 m, tall. The 14th Dalai Lama laid its foundation in 1997 and it was completed in 2004. It stands on a hilltop above Namchi and is visible from many points in and around the town, including the road from Jorethang.

faqs.q: How far is Samdruptse from Namchi town?
faqs.a: Samdruptse is a short drive from the Namchi bazaar, usually 15–20 minutes by taxi up a winding hill road. Most visitors hire a local taxi for a half day and combine it with Char Dham at Solophok, paying about ₹1,500–2,500 in total. Fit walkers can walk up, but the road is steep and has traffic.

faqs.q: Is Samdruptse worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially early on a clear morning. You get one of Sikkim's largest Buddhist statues, quiet paths with prayer flags, and wide views over the Rangeet valley to the Kanchenjunga range. The visit takes 1.5–2 hours. It is easy for families and older travellers, with paved paths and some steps, and pairs well with Char Dham.

experiences.title: Char Dham pilgrimage complex at Solophok
experiences.image_query: Char Dham Solophok Namchi Shiva statue
experiences.summary: Visit Siddheshwar Dham at Solophok, where a 108 ft seated Shiva rises over replicas of the four dhams and the 12 jyotirlingas. Opened in 2011, it lets pilgrims who cannot travel across India see all of them in one hilltop morning.
body: Char Dham, officially Siddheshwar Dham, sits on Solophok hill a short drive from Namchi. It was built by the Sikkim government and opened in 2011. The centrepiece is a seated Shiva about 108 ft tall, painted in blue and white on a raised base. Around it are replicas of the four dhams of Hindu pilgrimage, Badrinath, Dwarka, Jagannath Puri and Rameswaram, and of all 12 jyotirlinga shrines. Smaller shrines fill the gaps, and the hill looks out over the valleys towards the Rangeet and Teesta.

For many visiting families this is the main reason to come to Namchi, and the complex is built for pilgrims of every age. Paths are paved, there are steps and ramps, shoe counters, drinking water and toilets. Walk around the dhams in order and you pass through architectural styles from across India, scaled down but carefully made. Shoes come off at the entrance, and photography rules vary inside the shrines; follow the signs and the staff.

Go in the morning, when the light is good and crowds are lighter, and allow 1.5–2 hours. Festival days such as Maha Shivaratri and the monsoon month of Shravan bring large crowds, which is wonderful for atmosphere but slow for visiting. Entry is a small fee, roughly ₹50–100 for Indians, with separate rates for foreign nationals; check current status before you travel. Combine it with Samdruptse in a half-day taxi for about ₹1,500–2,500.

faqs.q: What is Char Dham in Namchi?
faqs.a: Char Dham, or Siddheshwar Dham, is a Hindu pilgrimage complex at Solophok near Namchi, opened in 2011. A seated Shiva about 108 ft tall stands at its centre, surrounded by replicas of the four dhams, Badrinath, Dwarka, Jagannath Puri and Rameswaram, and the 12 jyotirlingas. It lets pilgrims see all of them in one visit.

faqs.q: What are Char Dham Namchi's timings and entry fee?
faqs.a: Char Dham usually opens in the morning and closes in the evening, with a small entry fee of roughly ₹50–100 for Indian visitors and a different rate for foreign nationals. Timings, fees and photography rules change and festival days have special arrangements, so check at the gate or with your hotel before you go.

faqs.q: Is Char Dham suitable for elderly visitors?
faqs.a: Yes, it is one of the easier pilgrimage sites in the hills. Paths are paved, there are ramps as well as steps, and toilets and drinking water are on site. Some sections still involve climbs, so older visitors should go slowly and rest in the shade. Avoid major festival days if crowds are a concern.

experiences.title: Walk up Tendong, the Lepcha flood hill
experiences.summary: A forest walk from Damthang to the top of Tendong Hill, about 2,600 m, the sacred hill that Lepcha elders say rose to save their people from a great flood. At the top a watchtower gives one of the widest views in South Sikkim on a clear morning.
body: Tendong Hill rises between Namchi, Damthang and Ravangla to about 2,600 m. For the Lepcha people it is sacred. Lepcha elders tell that in a great flood the people climbed Tendong and the hill rose above the water to save them, until prayers made the flood recede. The name is usually translated as "upraised horn". Every 8 August Lepcha communities mark Tendong Lho Rum Faat with prayers to the hill, and some families still climb it that day.

Most walkers start from Damthang, on the hill road above Namchi towards Ravangla and Temi, about 45 minutes from Namchi by car. A forest trail of about 6 km climbs through oak, rhododendron, magnolia and bamboo; it is steady and mostly well defined, with a few steep stretches, and takes about 3 hours up and 2 down. Birds are plentiful in the early morning. On top is a clearing with a watchtower and prayer flags, and on clear days the view stretches across Sikkim to the Kanchenjunga range.

Start by 7 am from Damthang so you reach the top before cloud rises. Carry 2 litres of water, food, a rain layer and a warm top; there are no shops on the trail. A local guide, roughly ₹1,500–2,000 for the day, is helpful where paths branch, and a small forest fee may apply. Ask about current trail conditions before you travel. A reserved car Namchi–Damthang and back costs roughly ₹1,500–2,500 with waiting.

faqs.q: How long is the Tendong Hill trek?
faqs.a: From Damthang the trail is about 6 km one way and climbs to the top at about 2,600 m. Most walkers take about 3 hours up and 2 hours down, so plan for 5–6 hours including a rest at the top. It is a moderate day walk on a forest path; fit families with teenagers can manage it with an early start.

faqs.q: Where does the Tendong Hill trek start?
faqs.a: Most people start at Damthang, a small settlement on the hill road above Namchi towards Ravangla and Temi, about 45 minutes by car from Namchi. Shared jeeps between Namchi and Ravangla or Gangtok pass through Damthang, but a reserved car is easier for an early start. Ask locally for the trailhead, which is near the roadside.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Tendong Hill?
faqs.a: Lepcha elders tell that long ago a great flood covered the land, and the Lepcha people took refuge on Tendong Hill. As the waters rose, the hill rose with them and saved the people, until prayers and offerings made the flood go down. Lepcha communities remember this every 8 August with the festival of Tendong Lho Rum Faat.

experiences.title: A morning food walk in Namchi bazaar
experiences.summary: Walk the Namchi bazaar early, when sel roti comes out of the oil and the vegetable sellers set out greens, churpi and chillies. A cheap, filling way to taste South Sikkim's everyday food, finished with momos and a look at the spice stalls.
body: Namchi's bazaar is busiest in the morning, when shopkeepers open shutters and villagers bring in vegetables, greens and dairy. Start with sel roti, the ring-shaped bread made from a sweetened rice batter and fried in oil, eaten with tea or with a spicy potato curry. A plate costs little, and the first batch of the day is the best. Small tea shops serve milky tea for about ₹20–30 a glass and know who makes the freshest rotis on the street.

Then look at what the farms around Namchi produce. Market women sell bundles of mustard leaves, nettle, squash shoots and fiddlehead ferns, called ningro, in season. You will see soft churpi, a fresh cottage cheese, and hard churpi blocks made from yak or cow milk, both kept for cooking or chewing. Dalle khursani, the small round chilli of Sikkim, is sold fresh and pickled. Gundruk, fermented and dried greens, goes into soups and sour side dishes.

For lunch, sit down for momos, thukpa or a full thali in one of the bazaar restaurants, at about ₹80–250 a plate. Ask whether there is nettle soup or a gundruk dish that day. Pickles and large cardamom make light, practical souvenirs; buy sealed packets for travel. Avoid plastic bags, which Sikkim restricts, and carry a cloth bag. Prices here are lower than in Gangtok or Pelling, so it is a good place to stock up.

faqs.q: What local food should I try in Namchi?
faqs.a: Try sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread, with tea or potato curry in the morning; momos and thukpa at lunch; and, if you can find them, nettle soup, gundruk soup and dishes with churpi, the local cheese. Dalle khursani chilli pickle is the local heat. Thalis with rice, dal and seasonal greens are cheap and filling.

faqs.q: How much does food cost in Namchi?
faqs.a: Food in Namchi is cheaper than in Gangtok or Pelling. Indicatively, tea costs ₹20–30, a plate of momos ₹80–150, and a thali ₹150–250. Sel roti and snacks from bazaar stalls cost very little. A full day of simple meals can come to ₹400–700 per person if you eat where local people eat.

faqs.q: What can I buy in Namchi market?
faqs.a: Look for large cardamom, dalle chilli pickles, hard churpi, local tea from nearby Temi, and dried greens such as gundruk. Buy sealed packets of pickles and spices for the journey home. Sikkim restricts plastic bags, so carry a cloth bag. Prices are fair and fixed in most shops, with little bargaining needed.

faqs.q: What is Namchi famous for?
faqs.a: Namchi is known for the 118 ft Guru Padmasambhava statue on Samdruptse hill, the Char Dham pilgrimage complex at Solophok with its 108 ft Shiva, and Tendong Hill, sacred to the Lepcha people. It is also the headquarters town of Namchi district, the old South Sikkim, with a busy bazaar and frequent jeep links.

faqs.q: How do I reach Namchi from Siliguri or NJP?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Namchi for about ₹250–350 a seat and take 3.5–4 hours for the roughly 100 km drive. You can also take a jeep to Jorethang and change for Namchi, a further 45 minutes and ₹60–90. A reserved small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs roughly ₹4,000–5,000. Book jeep seats early in holiday weeks.

faqs.q: How far is Namchi from Gangtok and Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Namchi is about 3 hours by road from Gangtok, via Singtam or via Melli, and about 3 hours from Darjeeling via Jorethang. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok in the morning; from Darjeeling, a reserved car is simpler, or a jeep to Jorethang followed by a short jeep to Namchi. Check road status in the monsoon.

faqs.q: Is one day enough for Namchi?
faqs.a: One full day covers Samdruptse and Char Dham by taxi in the morning, with time for the Rock Garden and the bazaar after lunch. Add a second day if you want to climb Tendong Hill from Damthang. Many travellers see Namchi's sights on the way between Siliguri and Ravangla and sleep in Ravangla.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Namchi?
faqs.a: October to May. Autumn and early winter give clear skies and Kanchenjunga views; spring brings flowers and warm days. Namchi is lower and milder than Ravangla or Pelling, so December and January are pleasant rather than harsh. June to September brings heavy rain, low cloud and occasional landslides on the roads, so plan with spare time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Namchi?
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a permit for Namchi or anywhere in South Sikkim. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit before entering the state, available online as an e-RAP or at entry points such as Melli and Rangpo. Rules change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Samdruptse and Char Dham in half a day?
faqs.a: Yes. A local taxi from the Namchi bazaar can take you to Samdruptse and Char Dham at Solophok in 3.5–4.5 hours, including about 1.5 hours at each site. Expect to pay roughly ₹1,500–2,500 for the half day. Start around 8 am for clearer views and fewer people, and agree the stops and waiting time first.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Namchi on a budget?
faqs.a: Stay near the central bazaar and jeep stand, where budget hotels charge about ₹1,200–2,500 a night outside holiday weeks and food is close by. Look at the room before paying, as standards vary. For homestays and a cooler night, consider Ravangla or the villages near Temi, both within about an hour, and visit Namchi as a day trip.

faqs.q: When is Tendong Lho Rum Faat celebrated?
faqs.a: Tendong Lho Rum Faat is celebrated every year on 8 August. Lepcha communities offer prayers to Tendong Hill, which their tradition says saved their ancestors from a great flood, and some climb the hill that day. It falls in the monsoon, so expect rain and plan road travel with time to spare. Check local programmes before you travel.
